latin.276: GAR. 4. Imputatio primi peccati colligitur non ex eo simpliciter, quod omnes sunt ab Adamo oriundi, sed ex eo quod ita docemur ab Apostolo Roman. v. ut audivimus, & quod per peccatum illud excussit Adamus gratiam omnem foederis illius primarii, quod in ipso cum omnibus hominibus initum fuerat, ut saepius dictum. PLAC. Non docemur ab Apostolo Rom. 5. imputationem immediatam primi peccati. Id hactenus neque vir doctus, neque alius quisquam probavit, ut partim ex dictis, partim ex dicendis cernere est. Addit alteram rationem, sed eam non intelligo. Velim enim mihi exponi quale foedus in Adamo cum omnibus hominibus initum intelligat. Nam si ea fuisse conditione censet, ut, si peccaret Adamus, imputaretur ejus primum peccatum actuale omnibus ejus posteris immediate; id foedus adferendum non fuit ad probandam imputationem immediatam. Non enim minus in quaestione versatur quam illa ipsa imputatio: deque eo merito quaeri potest, undenam habeatur? Ex naturae inspectione? An ex divina per Scripturam revelatione? Aliunde enim si habetur, ob id ipsum rejici debet.
latin.277: Visne omnes homines considerari ut unam rempublicam, unum corpus, cujus caput sit Adamus, reliqui autem homines singuli membra? Fuit igitur Adamus caput sine corpore, ut nos hodie membra sine capite. GAR. Hoc rationis genus, si L. Crasso venisset in mentem ea dissertatione quam habuit cum Q. Mutio Scaevola apud Tullium lib. 1. de Oratore, non poterat ille plausibili argumento dictum Scaevolae traducere, Socratem vocantis fontem & caput Philosophorum, qui longa serie post exemptum humanis Socratem in Graecia floruerunt: nimirum, quia & Socrates ante natos illos Philosophos fons fuisset sine rivulis, & caput sine membris; & illi post Socratem Philosophi, rivi fuissent absque fonte, & membra sine capite.
latin.278: PLAC. Egregiam refutationem! Agebatur de Adamo relatè ad id tempus, quo primum peccavit, diu antequam nobis gignendis operam daret. Dixi eum tunc nondum fuisse caput nostrum, quomodo exercitus caput est dux, reipublicae magistratus, regni rex: quia caput fuisset sine membris. Num eo sensu Socratem Scaevola fontem & caput appellavit? Num ejus temporis respectu, cum nondum ullus esset ejus auditor, ullusve alius praeter eum philosophus? Num propterea aliqua Socratis actio omnibus aliis philosophis imputari immediate potuit aut debuit? Nihil quicquam a Socrate in sequentes philosophos imputatione descendit. GAR. Atqui si rem serio agimus, quidni vulgatissimam distinctionem in memoriam revocamus, ut caput proprie dictum discernatur ab improprie dicto, id est, physicum a morali? Nam in physico certe capite, quod natura suis nervis & vinculis cum reliquo corpore colligavit, ita res habet, ut neque caput dicetur, nisi cum adsunt membra; neque membra του παντός vocentur, nisi quae actu cum capite conjuncta sunt. At vero cum Adamum dicunt Theologi esse generis humani caput, impropriam sine dubio significationem usurpant, ut denotent originem esse & principium seminale generis humani, unde scilicet humana natura sumpserit initium. Quomodo scilicet Abrahamus Judaicae gentis caput dicitur.
latin.279: PLAC. Putavitne Vir Doctus me ita insanivisse ut caput proprie dictum intellexerim, qui disertis verbis dixi corpus improprie dictum, seu morale, tanquam rempublicam? Manifestum enim est rempublicam non esse corpus physicum: Et tamen, quamvis natura rempublicam cum capite suo rege, vel magistratu non colligaverit nervis & vinculis, nemo dixerit hominem tunc fuisse caput reipublicae, cum ipse viveret privatus, nondum nata republica: neque respublica quae nunc est corpus dicetur illius principis, qui ante centum aut mille annos desiit esse in vivis. Tale caput, tale corpus politicum intellexi. Nam alioqui non nego, neque negavi unquam, quin sit Adamus caput generis humani eo sensu quem Vir doctus hoc loco exponit. Sed quid ad immediatam imputationem peccati Adamici facit ista capitis ratio? An sic caput fuit Adamus duntaxat dum peccavit? An propterea quod Abrahamus gentis Judaicae caput fuit, eo modo ejus aliqua actio omnibus & singulis Judaeis imputatur?
latin.280: Et omnia peccata Adami nobis, nostra vicissim omnia Adamo imputari debuerunt; par enim est ratio: conveniunt enim toti corpori & quae capitis, & quae aliorum membrorum sunt. Me etiam perturbant ista verba, considerantur tanquam unus homo in Adamo; videris enim illum unum hominem ab Adamo distinguere. Porro quaecunque illa consideratio fuerit, cum ea extra nos esset, nec quicquam vel in Adamo, vel in nobis poneret, capere animo non possum, quid ad hoc contulerit, ut nos revera commiserimus peccatum illud actuale Adami tanto ante quam essemus. Adde quod si committente alia peccata Adamo perduravit, quid est quamobrem illa quoque nobis pariter non imputentur? Sin dum solum primum illud admitteret, obtinuit, mirabor, aut desiisse nos esse in Adamo confestim post primum illud peccatum admissum, aut, quamvis in eo ut antea essemus, non fuisse tamen amplius consideratos tanquam unum hominem in ipso. Subjicis nos peccasse in Adamo. Vide quam non sim difficilis, tibi id concedo, modo hoc etiam mihi concedas nos eo modo peccasse in Adamo, quo in eo fuimus. In eo autem fuimus, non quia ejus esse nobis imputetur, aut sit causa meritoria cur sumus, sed quia nos propagatione naturali per intermedios nostros parentes genuit: Eodem modo nos in eo peccasse confiteor, quia peccatum ejus nostrum peccatum longa propagationum serie procreavit.
latin.281: Caeterum hanc tuam responsionem interrogationibus firmas. Nam, inquis, qui potest aliter reddi ratio hujus infectionis & reatus? cur quaeso Adam peccando perdidit, & morti subjecit, non tantum personam, sed etiam totam naturam humanam? Cum caeteri homines peccatis suis actualibus laedant personas, & se mortis reos efficiant. Qui potest nobis peccatum actuale juste imputari, quod neque fecimus ipsi, neque jussimus, neque suasimus, neque ullo voluntatis nostrae consensu probavimus, quodque nostro respectu nullo modo voluntarium fuit? Horumne tu rationem reddere potes? Annon igitur satius esset propagationem corruptionis inhaerentis & reatus qui eam sequitur, docente Scriptura, contestante experientia, firmiter credere; modum autem quem non capis Deo permittere, quam praeter & contra Scripturam imputationem excogitare aeque, aut magis difficilem captu, ac Dei justitiam pervertentem, & maculantem?

pass_a.276: GAR 4: first-sin imputation is not drawn merely from being born of Adam, but from what Rom. 5 teaches (as already heard) and from Adam's shaking off all the grace of that primary covenant struck in him with all men. PLAC: Rom. 5 does not teach immediate imputation of the first sin—neither the learned man nor anyone else has proved that yet, as partly appears from what was said and partly from what remains. He adds another reason I do not understand. I want him to explain what covenant in Adam with all men he means. If he takes it as conditioned that if Adam sinned his first actual sin would be immediately imputed to all posterity, that covenant was not to be brought in to prove immediate imputation—it is no less in question than the imputation itself. Whence is it had—from inspecting nature, or from divine revelation in Scripture? If from elsewhere, it should be rejected for that very reason.
pass_a.277: Shall everyone be treated as one commonwealth and one body under Adam as head, each other person a limb? Then at the first sin Adam would be a head with no body, and we now limbs with no head. GAR answers by recalling Crassus versus Scaevola in Cicero's De Oratore book 1: the same style of objection could have mocked calling Socrates the spring and head of later Greek philosophers—Socrates a spring without brooks and a head without limbs before they existed, and they afterward brooks without a spring and limbs without a head.
pass_a.278: PLAC: Fine rebuttal! We were speaking of Adam at the hour of his first fall, ages before he fathered us. I denied he was already our head then in the way a commander heads an army, a magistrate a city, or a king a realm—because that would be a head with no limbs. Is that how Scaevola named Socrates spring and head? Relative to a moment when he had no pupil and no fellow philosopher? Must some deed of Socrates therefore be charged at once to every later philosopher? No imputed inheritance ran from Socrates to those who followed. GAR: Taking the matter in earnest, recover the usual split between head in the proper (physical) sense and head improperly (morally). A physical head is nerve-bound to its body, so neither head nor members of the whole exist without actual junction. When theologians call Adam head of humankind they mean the improper sense: origin and seed-principle of the race from which human nature began—as Abraham is head of the Jewish nation.
pass_a.279: PLAC: Did he imagine I meant a literal physical head, though I expressly named an improper or moral body like a commonwealth? A commonwealth is not a physical body; still, no one calls a private man the commonwealth's head before the commonwealth exists, nor calls today's state the body of a prince dead for centuries. That political head and body is my meaning. Apart from that I never denied Adam is head of the race in the learned man's present sense. Yet how does that head-account secure immediate imputation of Adam's sin? Was he head in that sense only while sinning? Does Abraham's headship of the Jews mean some one act of Abraham is charged that way to every Jew?
pass_a.280: By the same body-logic every sin of Adam should fall on us and every sin of ours on him, since head and members share what belongs to the whole. The phrase 'regarded as one man in Adam' also unsettles me—you appear to split that one man from Adam himself. Whatever the regard was, being outside us and adding nothing in Adam or in us, I cannot see how it made us truly do Adam's actual deed ages before we were. If the regard lasted through Adam's later sins, why are those not charged to us alike? If it held only for the first, I marvel either that we left Adam the moment after that first sin, or that though still in him we were no longer regarded as one man in him. You say we sinned in Adam. I grant it if we sinned in him only as we were in him: not by his being imputed to us or meriting our existence, but because natural generation through our intervening parents came from him. Just so I confess we sinned in him: his sin, through a long chain of generations, brought forth our sin.
pass_a.281: You then prop the reply with queries: how else explain this infection and guilt? Why did Adam's fall ruin and doom to death not a lone person but human nature as a whole, when other men's actual sins only wound persons and make themselves death-guilty? How is an actual sin justly laid on us that we never did, ordered, urged, or willed, and that was involuntary for us? Can you answer those? Better, then, to hold fast the spread of inborn corruption and the guilt that follows—Scripture teaching it, experience confirming it—and leave the ungrasped mode to God, than to mint, beside and against Scripture, an imputation still harder to grasp that twists and soils divine justice.

276: GAR. 4. The imputation of the first sin is gathered not simply from the fact that all are sprung from Adam, but from this: that we are so taught by the Apostle in Romans 5, as we have heard, and that by that sin Adam shook off all the grace of that primary covenant which had been struck in him with all men, as has often been said. PLAC. We are not taught by the Apostle in Rom. 5 the immediate imputation of the first sin. That neither the learned man nor anyone else has thus far proved, as may be seen partly from what has been said and partly from what is to be said. He adds another reason, but I do not understand it. For I would have him explain to me what covenant struck in Adam with all men he understands. For if he judges it to have been on this condition, that if Adam sinned his first actual sin would be immediately imputed to all his posterity, that covenant ought not to have been brought forward to prove immediate imputation. For it is no less in question than that imputation itself; and concerning it one may rightly ask whence it is had. From inspection of nature? Or from divine revelation through Scripture? For if it is had from elsewhere, for that very reason it ought to be rejected.
277: Do you want all men to be considered as one republic, one body, whose head is Adam, and the remaining men each members? Then Adam was a head without a body, as we today are members without a head. GAR. This kind of reasoning, if it had come into L. Crassus's mind in that dissertation which he held with Q. Mucius Scaevola in Cicero, On the Orator, book 1, he could not by a plausible argument have turned aside Scaevola's saying that calls Socrates the fountain and head of the philosophers who in a long series flourished in Greece after Socrates was removed from human affairs—namely, because Socrates before those philosophers were born would have been a fountain without streams and a head without members; and those philosophers after Socrates would have been streams without a fountain and members without a head.
278: PLAC. An excellent refutation! The discussion concerned Adam with reference to that time when he first sinned, long before he set himself to begetting us. I said that he was not yet then our head, as a general is head of an army, a magistrate of a republic, a king of a kingdom—because he would have been a head without members. Did Scaevola call Socrates fountain and head in that sense? With respect to that time, when there was not yet any hearer of his, nor any other philosopher besides him? Could or ought some action of Socrates therefore to be immediately imputed to all other philosophers? Nothing whatever descended from Socrates to the following philosophers by imputation. GAR. But if we treat the matter seriously, why should we not recall the most common distinction, so that head properly so called may be discerned from that improperly so called—that is, the physical from the moral? For in a physical head, which nature has bound by its nerves and ties with the rest of the body, the matter stands so that neither will it be called a head unless members are present, nor will members of the whole be so called unless they are actually joined with the head. But when theologians say Adam is the head of the human race, they without doubt use an improper signification, to denote that he is the origin and seminal principle of the human race, from which of course human nature took its beginning. Just as Abraham is called the head of the Jewish people.
279: PLAC. Did the learned man think I had so lost my mind as to understand a head properly so called, when I said in express words an improperly so called, or moral, body, as a republic? For it is plain that a republic is not a physical body. And yet, although nature has not bound a republic to its kingly or magisterial head by nerves and ties, no one would say that a man was then head of the republic when he himself lived as a private person, the republic not yet born; nor will the republic which now is be called the body of that prince who a hundred or a thousand years ago ceased to be among the living. Such a head, such a political body, I understood. For otherwise I do not deny, nor have I ever denied, that Adam is the head of the human race in that sense which the learned man explains in this place. But what does that account of the head do for the immediate imputation of Adam's sin? Was Adam head in that way only while he sinned? Or because Abraham was head of the Jewish people, is some action of his in that way imputed to all and each of the Jews?
280: And all Adam's sins ought to have been imputed to us, and all ours in turn to Adam; for the reason is equal: for what belongs to the head and what belongs to the other members suit the whole body. Those words also disturb me—'they are considered as one man in Adam'; for you seem to distinguish that one man from Adam. Further, whatever that consideration was, since it was outside us and put nothing either in Adam or in us, I cannot grasp in mind what it contributed to this—that we truly committed that actual sin of Adam so long before we existed. Add that if it endured while Adam was committing other sins, why are those also not equally imputed to us? But if it obtained only while he admitted that first one, I shall marvel either that we ceased to be in Adam immediately after that first sin was admitted, or that, although we were in him as before, we were nevertheless no longer considered as one man in him. You subjoin that we sinned in Adam. See how little difficult I am: I grant you that, provided you also grant me that we sinned in Adam in the same way in which we were in him. Now we were in him not because his being is imputed to us, or is a meritorious cause why we exist, but because by natural propagation through our intermediate parents he begot us. In the same way I confess that we sinned in him, because his sin by a long series of propagations begot our sin.
281: For the rest, you shore up this answer of yours with questions. For, you say, who can otherwise give the reason of this infection and guilt? Why, I ask, did Adam by sinning destroy and subject to death not only a person but also the whole human nature—whereas other men by their actual sins wound persons and make themselves liable to death? How can an actual sin be justly imputed to us which we ourselves neither did, nor ordered, nor advised, nor approved by any consent of our will, and which with respect to us was in no way voluntary? Can you give the reason of these things? Would it not then be better firmly to believe the propagation of inherent corruption and of the guilt which follows it—Scripture teaching, experience bearing witness—and to leave to God the mode which you do not grasp, than beside and against Scripture to invent an imputation equally, or more, hard to grasp, and one that perverts and stains the justice of God?
